fastRead: A teenager scooping cones at a Baskin-Robbins can be sleepwalking or building a career, and the only difference is intention. To act with intention is to do even the smallest task thoughtfully, for a clear purpose, with the result you want in view. The kid who treats the scoop as if it matters is practicing excellence before anyone hands him a title. The one who coasts is just passing time. Excellence is not a function of position; it is a function of intention. Choosing it in the lowest-status job is what builds the foundation everything else stands on.
deepRead: Why does treating a trivial task as if it matters compound into something big? Because intention is a habit, and habits practiced on small things hold up on large ones. A string of deliberately chosen early jobs makes the point. At sixteen, bussing tables at Wolfgang Puck's Spago was not a random first paycheck. It was a chosen rung, taken because a destination had already been named: study hospitality at Cornell, then one day open a restaurant in New York. With the end in view, every job in between could be aimed rather than merely accepted. None of this was accidental. A father who had spent a life in restaurants stayed involved well past graduation, helping pick each role specifically to build the strongest foundation, so intention was modeled before it was consciously chosen. The deeper move underneath the stories is to start with the result you actually want, including the feeling you want a person to leave with, and let the task follow from that. A clear destination is what makes every small choice point the same direction.
fullRead: Intention is easy to confuse with hard work, and the difference is the whole point. You can grind long hours, loyally, in a humble role and still be sleepwalking through it. Effort measures how much you do. Intention measures whether you do it on purpose, for a result you can name. A line cook pulling doubles can be coasting; a scooper at an ice cream counter can be wide awake. Hours are not the proxy; purpose is. The uncomfortable demand is that no role is too small to be done with intention, which removes the usual excuse for coasting while you wait to be promoted. You can behave like a leader and an innovator while still washing dishes. The title is permission you do not actually need. Acting with excellence before anyone grants you authority is what builds both a career and a culture, because the standard you hold on the invisible jobs is the standard you will hold on the visible ones. The discipline travels into any work. A new analyst, a guard in a quiet museum, a clerk processing forms, each can decide the result they want, including how the person on the other side should feel, and do the task as if it depends on it. The move is the same everywhere: name the outcome first, then let the tactic follow, and check whether the person felt understood in a specific way rather than merely served. That single shift, from task-first to outcome-first, quietly turns busywork into craft. The same discipline can be modeled and taught, the way a parent who picks each early job on purpose teaches a child to sequence experiences rather than take whatever comes along. Intention learned that way becomes a reflex: you stop asking whether a task is worth your full attention and simply give it, because that is who you have decided to be at work. It shows up first on the jobs no one notices, the swept floor, the careful handoff, the email written as if it matters, and those quiet reps are what make the visible work look effortless later. The limit is worth stating plainly. Intention is not a speech about caring or a one-time burst of effort. It is a quiet habit applied to the trivial tasks nobody is watching. The honest test is whether a team can take a routine, low-status job and do it with real purpose, day after day, without needing an audience. When it can, intention has stopped being a value on a wall and become the way the work is actually done, the foundation everything more impressive is later built on.
